notes.subtitle: Lines, Boundaries, Regions & Circle Vocabulary

concepts.title: Line family
concepts.text: A line extends endlessly in both directions, a ray begins at one endpoint, and a line segment is bounded by two endpoints.

concepts.title: Figures and regions
concepts.text: An open figure has a gap; a closed figure has a complete boundary that separates its interior from its exterior.

concepts.title: Boundaries and vertices
concepts.text: A linear boundary uses line segments and a curvilinear boundary uses curves; one boundary may contain both kinds. Two rays with a common vertex form an angle, whose interior is the region between its arms and whose exterior is the remaining region.

concepts.title: Polygons and circles
concepts.text: A triangle has sides, vertices, angles, interior and exterior, a median from a vertex to the opposite midpoint, and an altitude perpendicular to the opposite side. A convex quadrilateral has sides, vertices, angles, diagonals, adjacent and opposite sides, interior and exterior. Circle vocabulary includes centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, sector, segment, semicircle and circumference.

formulas: Triangle median: vertex to midpoint of opposite side
Triangle altitude: perpendicular from vertex to opposite side
method: Check whether the figure has endpoints or a complete boundary.
Identify straight, curved or mixed parts of the boundary.
Name vertices and sides in their order around the figure.
For a circle, first locate the centre and then decide whether a segment is a radius, chord or diameter.

example.question: In a circle with centre O, AB passes through O and has endpoints on the circle; OP joins O to the circle. Name AB and OP if AB = 12 cm.
steps: AB is a chord through the centre, so it is a diameter.
OP joins the centre to the circle, so it is a radius.
A radius is half a diameter: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
example.answer: AB is a 12 cm diameter and OP is a 6 cm radius.

practice.question: How many endpoints do a line, ray and segment have?
Classify a triangle as open or closed and its boundary as linear or curvilinear.
In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of BC and AE ⟂ BC. Name AD and AE.
practice.answer: AD is a median and AE is an altitude.

practice.question: A circle has radius 7.5 cm. Find its diameter.
Distinguish a sector from a segment of a circle.
practice.answer: A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc; a segment is bounded by a chord and its arc.

practice.question: For convex quadrilateral PQRS, list its sides and diagonals, name one pair each of adjacent and opposite sides, and locate a point enclosed by its boundary.
practice.answer: Sides PQ, QR, RS, SP; diagonals PR, QS; for example PQ and QR are adjacent, while PQ and RS are opposite; an enclosed point lies in the interior.

tips: A segment is finite even though the line containing it extends endlessly.
A closed figure separates interior from exterior; for an angle, the region between its arms is the interior and the remaining region is the exterior.
Every diameter is a chord, but not every chord is a diameter.

notes.subtitle: Measurement, Classification & Polygon Families

concepts.title: Measurement and line relationships
concepts.text: Use a ruler from its zero mark for segments and a protractor from the correct zero scale for angles. Lines may be parallel, intersecting or perpendicular.

concepts.title: Angle types
concepts.text: Angles are classified by their measure as zero, acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex or complete.

concepts.title: Triangles
concepts.text: By sides, triangles are scalene, isosceles or equilateral; by angles, they are acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled.

concepts.title: Quadrilaterals and polygons
concepts.text: Trapezium, parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and square are identified by side and angle properties. Polygons from three to eight sides have standard names; a regular polygon has all sides and all angles equal, while a non-regular polygon does not.

formulas: Zero angle: θ = 0°; acute angle: 0° < θ < 90°
method: Measure the required segment or angle with the instrument aligned at zero.
Compare the result with the defining lengths, angle ranges or parallel-side conditions.
Classify a triangle separately by sides and by angles when enough information is given.
State the most specific quadrilateral or polygon name and verify every defining property.

example.question: A triangle has two equal sides, and the included angle between them measures 100°. Classify it.
steps: Two sides are equal, so it is isosceles by sides.
One angle is greater than 90° and less than 180°, so it is obtuse-angled.
Combine both descriptions.

practice.question: Classify 0°, 72°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 250° and 360°.
practice.answer: Zero, acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex, complete

practice.answer: Hexagon, heptagon, octagon; a regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal.

practice.question: Explain why every square is both a rectangle and a rhombus.
practice.answer: It has four right angles like a rectangle and four equal sides like a rhombus

tips: Read the protractor scale that begins at the aligned arm.
Equal sides and equal angles describe different triangle classifications.
Choose the most specific name: a four-equal-sided right-angled quadrilateral is a square.

notes.subtitle: Solids, Elements & Foldable Nets

concepts.title: Recognising solids
concepts.text: A cube, cuboid, cylinder, sphere and cone can be identified by their flat faces, curved surfaces, bases and corners. Prisms and pyramids are named from the shapes of their bases.

concepts.title: Faces, edges and vertices
concepts.text: A face is a flat surface, an edge is where faces meet, and a vertex is a corner where edges meet. For curved solids, distinguish flat faces from curved surfaces and circular edges.

concepts.title: Prisms and pyramids
concepts.text: A prism has two congruent parallel bases joined by side faces. A pyramid has one base and triangular side faces meeting at one apex; a tetrahedron is a triangular pyramid.

concepts.title: Nets
concepts.text: A net is a flat arrangement of faces that folds without overlap to make a solid. Different valid nets may form the same solid.

method: Identify the shape and number of its bases.
Count flat faces first, then edges and vertices systematically.
For a net, match every piece with a face or curved surface of the solid.
Mentally fold adjoining edges and check that no faces overlap or remain open.

example.question: Describe a triangular prism and the pieces in its net.
steps: Identify its two congruent triangular bases.
The three pairs of corresponding base edges are joined by three rectangular faces.
Count all elements: F=5, E=9 and V=6.
example.answer: Its net contains two congruent triangles and three rectangles; the solid has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

practice.question: State F, E and V for a cube.
State F, E and V for a square pyramid.
Name a solid with one curved surface and no edge or vertex.
List the pieces in a closed-cylinder net.
practice.answer: One rectangle and two equal circles

practice.question: List the pieces in a cone net.
practice.answer: One circular sector and one circle

practice.question: Explain why four triangles can form a tetrahedron net.
practice.answer: One triangle is the base and three triangles fold up along its sides to meet and close the solid.

tips: Count every edge once, even though two faces meet there.
Use “flat face” and “curved surface” to avoid ambiguity for cones and cylinders.
A collection with the correct faces is a valid net only if it folds without overlap.

notes.subtitle: Reflection, Angles & Exact Constructions

concepts.title: Reflection symmetry
concepts.text: A line of symmetry acts like a mirror: each point and its image lie at equal perpendicular distances on opposite sides of the line.

concepts.title: Perpendicular bisector
concepts.text: A perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint of a segment at 90°. Every point on it is equidistant from the segment's endpoints.

concepts.title: Angle constructions
concepts.text: A protractor measures any required angle. Equal-radius compass arcs construct 60°, stepping twice gives 120°, and angle bisectors produce 30° and 45° from 60° and 90°.

concepts.title: Copying and circles
concepts.text: A compass transfers equal lengths and angles. A circle is determined by its centre and radius, so the compass opening must remain fixed while drawing it.

formulas: An angle bisector gives θ/2 and θ/2
method: Draw and label the base ray, line or segment accurately.
Use the stated centre and the same compass radius for matching arcs.
Join only the required points with a straightedge and keep construction arcs visible.
Measure or use symmetry properties to verify the completed construction.

example.question: Construct 60° at O and bisect it.
steps: Draw ray OA and an arc centred at O crossing OA at A.
With the same radius centred at A, mark B on the arc and join OB; ∠AOB=60°.
Draw equal arcs from A and B to meet at C, then join OC.
example.answer: OC bisects the 60° angle, producing two 30° angles.

practice.question: Draw AB=6.5 cm.
Construct the perpendicular bisector of a 10 cm segment.
practice.answer: It meets the segment at 5 cm and at 90°

practice.question: Construct 120° using a compass.
practice.answer: Step two equal 60° chords around an arc from the base ray

practice.question: Bisect a constructed 90° angle.
Reflect a point 4 cm from a mirror line.
practice.answer: Its image is 4 cm from the line on the opposite perpendicular

practice.question: Draw a circle with centre O and diameter 8 cm.

tips: Do not change the compass opening while drawing equal arcs.
Place the protractor centre exactly on the vertex and read from the correct zero.
Construction arcs are evidence of the method, so leave them visible.

notes.subtitle: Boundaries, Surfaces & Everyday Measures

concepts.title: Perimeter and area
concepts.text: Perimeter measures the distance around a closed figure in linear units. Area measures the surface covered inside it in square units.

concepts.title: Rectangles and squares
concepts.text: Use length and breadth for a rectangle. In a square all four sides are equal, so its rectangle formulae reduce to expressions involving one side.

concepts.title: Same perimeter, different area
concepts.text: Shapes can have an equal boundary length but different areas. For rectangles with a fixed perimeter, changing length and breadth can change their product.

concepts.title: Unit conversions
concepts.text: Convert quantities to the same unit before calculating. Multiply when changing to a smaller unit and divide when changing to a larger unit.

method: Draw or identify the shape and label every known dimension.
Decide whether the question asks for perimeter, area or a unit conversion.
Convert all quantities to compatible units and apply the correct formula.
Check the size of the answer and attach a linear or square unit as appropriate.

example.question: A rectangle 14 cm by 6 cm and a square have the same perimeter. Find the square’s side and compare their areas.
steps: Rectangle perimeter = 2(14 + 6) = 40 cm.
Square side = 40 ÷ 4 = 10 cm.
Rectangle area = 14 × 6 = 84 cm²; square area = 10² = 100 cm².
Difference = 100 − 84 = 16 cm².
example.answer: The square side is 10 cm, and its area is 16 cm² greater.

practice.question: Find the perimeter and area of a rectangle 11 cm by 7 cm.
A square has perimeter 44 m. Find its side and area.
Convert 3 kg 85 g to grams.
Convert 4 L 250 mL to millilitres.
A film begins at 2:40 p.m. and ends at 4:55 p.m. Find its duration.
A rectangle 13 cm by 7 cm and a square have perimeter 40 cm. Compare their areas.
practice.answer: Rectangle area = 91 cm²; square side = 10 cm and area = 100 cm²; square is greater by 9 cm².

tips: Perimeter uses units such as cm; area uses square units such as cm².
Convert first when measurements are written in mixed units.
Equal perimeters do not guarantee equal areas.

notes.subtitle: Tables, Scaled Graphs, Mean & Median

concepts.title: Collecting and organising data
concepts.text: Raw observations become easier to read when sorted into categories and recorded with tallies and frequencies. Each tally bundle of five supports quick counting.

concepts.title: Pictographs
concepts.text: A pictograph represents quantities with repeated symbols. Its key or scale must be used to translate each symbol into the number it represents.

concepts.title: Bar graphs
concepts.text: A bar graph uses equal-width bars and a uniform scale. A clear title, labelled axes and equal gaps make comparisons reliable.

concepts.title: Mean and median
concepts.text: The mean shares the total equally among all observations. The median is the middle after ordering; with an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.

formulas: Total observations = sum of all frequencies
Pictograph value = number of symbols × value of one symbol
Bar value = bar height in scale units × value of one unit
Mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations
Even-count median = sum of the two middle values ÷ 2
method: Collect the observations and arrange them when order is needed.
Use tallies or a frequency table to check that every observation is counted once.
Read the key or choose a convenient uniform scale before drawing a pictograph or bar graph.
Calculate mean or median carefully, then check it against the range of the data.

example.question: Find the mean and median of 4, 7, 5, 9, 5 and 6.
steps: Add the observations: 4 + 7 + 5 + 9 + 5 + 6 = 36.
Arrange the data: 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 9.

practice.question: Prepare a frequency table for 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 4.
If ◆ represents 5 trees, how many trees do 6 symbols represent?
Find the mean of 3, 6, 8, 5 and 8.
Find the median of 11, 5, 7, 9 and 6.
Find the median of 4, 10, 6, 8, 12 and 2.
Describe bar heights for A 15, B 25, C 10 and D 20 using scale 1 unit = 5.
practice.answer: A: 3 units, B: 5 units, C: 2 units, D: 4 units, with title and labelled axes.

tips: Always arrange observations before finding the median.
A graph is incomplete without a title, labels and a scale or key.
Check that the sum of frequencies equals the number of raw observations.
